summary: Allows TCP to start with a larger initial congestion window, up to roughly 4 kilobytes instead of one segment. It discusses the benefits and drawbacks, experiments showing no congestion collapse, and implementation advice. It replaces RFC 2414 and updates RFC 2581.

eli5.summary: TCP starts cautiously, like dipping a toe in water. This document says it may begin with a slightly bigger first step so small downloads finish faster.

subtitle: TCP may open a connection with up to four segments in flight instead of one or two, saving round trips on short transfers.

tldr.problem: A TCP connection that starts with only one or two segments wastes round trips and delayed-ACK timeouts, which hurts short transfers and long-delay links such as satellite paths.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC raises the permitted upper bound for the initial window to min (4*MSS, max (2*MSS, 4380 bytes)), roughly 4K bytes, and leaves the loss window at one segment.
tldr.outcome: The change is optional, and the RFC argues from simulations and experiments that it does not risk congestion collapse. It obsoletes RFC 2414 and updates RFC 2581.

facts.label: Loss window
facts.value: Stays at 1 segment of MSS bytes

facts.label: Delayed ACK wait avoided
facts.value: Often up to 200 msec, possibly up to 500 msec

today: RFC 3390 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 2414 and updates RFC 2581.

sections.title: The New Upper Bound
sections.content:
RFC 3390 raises the permitted upper bound for TCP's initial window from one or two segments to between two and four segments. In most cases that is roughly 4K bytes. The bound is given by min (4*MSS, max (2*MSS, 4380 bytes)), where MSS is the maximum segment size.

The change is optional: a TCP MAY start with a larger window, though the authors expect most general-purpose implementations to adopt the new bound. It replaces the rule in RFC 2581, which initialized the congestion window to one or two segments.

The larger window applies to the first round trip of data after the three-way handshake. The SYN/ACK and its acknowledgment must not raise the window above the bound. If the SYN or SYN/ACK is lost, the sender MUST use a window of one segment of MSS bytes.
sections.eli5: TCP used to be allowed to send one or two packages before waiting to hear back. Now it may send up to four, a bit like being allowed to carry a few more bags on the first trip.

sections.title: Implementation Issues
sections.content:
Only the initial window changes. TCP uses slow start in up to three ways: to start a connection (the initial window), to restart after a long idle period (the restart window) and to restart after a retransmit timeout (the loss window). A TCP MAY set the restart window to the minimum of the initial window and the current cwnd. The loss window MUST remain one segment of MSS bytes, so the lowest possible window is available in severe congestion.

When a larger initial window is combined with Path MTU Discovery and the MSS turns out to be too large, cwnd SHOULD be reduced by the ratio of the old segment size to the new one, to avoid bursts of small segments. The RFC calls it an open question whether to set the Don't Fragment bit on all initial segments or on just one, and says that setting it on the last segment minimises needless retransmissions.

The RFC also says the larger window is not encouragement for web browsers to open several simultaneous connections, each with a large initial window. It suggests persistent connections and pipelining in HTTP/1.1 instead.
sections.eli5: Only the very first step gets bigger. If something goes badly wrong, TCP still shrinks back to one tiny step.

sections.title: Advantages of Larger Initial Windows
sections.content:
The RFC lists three benefits. First, with a one-segment window a receiver using delayed ACKs must wait for a timeout before acknowledging, often up to 200 msec and possibly up to 500 msec. With at least two segments, the receiver acknowledges after the second one arrives.

Second, connections that send only a little data finish faster. For many email and web page transfers of less than 4K bytes, the larger window cuts the transfer to a single round-trip time (RTT).

Third, connections that will grow a large window skip up to three RTTs and a delayed-ACK timeout in the initial slow-start phase. The RFC singles out high-bandwidth, large-delay paths such as satellite links.
sections.eli5: If you can only send one letter at a time and must wait for a reply, a short message takes many trips. Sending a few letters at once gets it done in one trip.

sections.title: Costs and Risks
sections.content:
For a single connection, the downside appears in high-congestion environments, especially with Drop Tail router queues that dislike bursts. A connection starting with four segments may suffer drops, and so unnecessary retransmits, that a one-segment start would have avoided. These drops are unlikely in uncongested networks with enough buffering or where routers use active queue management such as Random Early Detection.

For the network, the RFC considers two congestion-collapse dangers: many duplicate segments, and many segments dropped later after using scarce bandwidth on earlier links. Appendix A argues the duplicates would be few, with at most one duplicate segment in the cases examined. The RFC also admits that a very high drop rate could rise further. Its judgment is that there is no danger of congestion collapse from raising the initial window to 4K bytes.

There is also a timer problem. On low-bandwidth paths the small handshake packets do not seed the retransmission timer well, so a bigger first burst can trigger a spurious timeout. The RFC leaves the choice to implementers but RECOMMENDS not sampling RTT during the three-way handshake and using limited transmit from RFC 3042. Finally, it notes that TCP is already bursty: bursts of two and three segments are typical.
sections.eli5: A bigger first step can sometimes make a crowded hallway jam up, and a slow walker may think nobody answered. The authors checked and decided the risks are small.

sections.title: Simulations and Experiments
sections.content:
The RFC surveys earlier studies. Over satellite links, an initial window of four segments with a 512 byte MSS gave throughput improvements of up to 30%, depending on transfer size. Over a dialup modem link, a four-segment window cut the transfer time of a 16KB file by roughly 10% with no rise in drop rate.

For effects on other traffic, tests of 16 KB transfers to 100 Internet hosts showed a small drop-rate increase of 0.04 segments per transfer and roughly 25% less transfer time. A simulation study found that, apart from one scenario, drop rates rose by less than 1%; in that scenario the rate went from 3.5% to 4.5%.

In a highly congested network, another experiment found loss rates 1-2% higher and more time waiting for retransmit timers. The RFC concludes that in a very congested environment, where each connection's share is close to one segment, a larger window can cause a perceptible increase in loss and timeouts.
sections.eli5: People tried it out in many pretend and real networks. Most of the time things got faster, and only in a badly jammed network did it cause a bit more trouble.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section is brief. It says that the document discusses the initial congestion window permitted for TCP connections, and that changing this value does not raise any known new security issues with TCP.
sections.eli5: Letting TCP take a slightly bigger first step does not give bad guys any new trick that anyone knows about.
